sec.title: Purpose:
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies have improved outcomes in patients with relapsed/refractory large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL). However, up to two thirds of these patients do not maintain long-term responses. The phase 1/2 ZUMA-6 study investigated the feasibility of combining the CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) with the PD-L1 inhibitor atezolizumab as a potential approach to increase treatment efficacy while maintaining acceptable safety.

sec.title: Patients and Methods:
sec.p: Patients with refractory diffuse LBCL received a single axi-cel infusion (2 × 106 cells/kg), followed by atezolizumab 1,200 mg i.v. every 21 days for four cycles. Primary endpoints were dose-limiting toxicities (phase 1) and complete response rate (phase 2). Other efficacy and safety outcomes and pharmacokinetics/pharmacodynamics were assessed.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: Overall, 34 patients received axi-cel plus atezolizumab in ZUMA-6. The median follow-up for the final analysis was 56.9 months. In phase 1, one patient experienced dose-limiting toxicities (grade 4 neutropenia and thrombocytopenia). Thirty patients (88%) experienced grade ≥3 treatment-emergent adverse events. Three (9%) and 11 (32%) patients experienced grade ≥3 cytokine release syndrome and neurologic events, respectively. In the final analysis, 15 patients (54%) had a complete response. The median progression-free survival and overall survival were 9 and 32.2 months, respectively. Peak CAR T-cell and cytokine profiles were comparable with those previously reported for axi-cel monotherapy (ZUMA-1).

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: Axi-cel plus atezolizumab had a manageable safety profile, with no new safety signals. Safety and efficacy of this combination were consistent with axi-cel monotherapy. Correlative analyses could inform with regard to which patients with LBCL may benefit from axi-cel and immune checkpoint inhibitor combinations.

boxed-text.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies have improved outcomes in refractory large B-cell lymphoma; however, relapse rates indicate that clinical benefit could be further extended. Tumor PD-L1 expression is associated with inferior survival outcomes. Additionally, in preclinical studies, PD-1 expression increased on CAR T cells after target cell binding, suggesting that inhibition of PD-1/PD-L1 signaling may enhance the efficacy of CAR T-cell therapies. We conducted a phase 1/2 study of the CD19-directed CAR T-cell therapy axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) in combination with the PD-L1 inhibitor atezolizumab. One patient experienced dose-limiting toxicities in phase 1, with no new safety signals. Both complete response rate and the proportion of patients who had ongoing responses with axi-cel plus atezolizumab were comparable with those previously reported for axi-cel monotherapy. Combinations of CAR T-cell therapies and immune checkpoint inhibitors remain potential avenues of investigation in patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. Results from this trial may help inform the design of future studies of CAR T-cell and immune checkpoint inhibitor combination therapies.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) is an autologous CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy approved for the treatment of adult patients with relapsed or refractory (R/R) large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) that was refractory to first-line chemoimmunotherapy or that relapsed within 12 months of first-line chemoimmunotherapy and in patients with LBCL after ≥2 lines of prior systemic therapy (1). Axi-cel is now recognized as a standard-of-care option for second-line therapy in patients with primary refractory LBCL or those with early relapse (within 12 months) and for third-line or later therapy in patients with late relapse (beyond 12 months; refs. 2–4). In the pivotal ZUMA-1 trial, patients with refractory LBCL after ≥2 lines of prior therapy achieved a median overall survival (OS) of 25.8 months and an objective response rate (ORR) of 83%, with a median follow-up of 63.1 months (5). In the ZUMA-7 trial, patients with early R/R LBCL after one prior line of therapy had a median event-free survival of 8.3 months and the median OS was not reached (ORR was 83%), with a median follow-up of 24.9 months (6). Despite the OS and objective responses observed in ZUMA-1, 70% of patients did not maintain long-term responses. Thus, although axi-cel provides durable remission for some patients, there is still a need to improve long-term outcomes for a larger proportion of patients.

Combination therapies to enhance CAR T-cell efficacy and the durability of responses, including combinations with chemotherapies, Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors, or immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI), are being explored (7, 8). PD-1 (expressed by T cells) and its ligand PD-L1 (expressed by antigen-presenting cells and tumor cells) negatively regulate T-cell responses, and the PD-1/PD-L1 signaling pathway is associated with T-cell exhaustion and reduced antitumor activity of T cells (9–11). ICIs, such as PD-1 inhibitors (e.g., pembrolizumab and nivolumab) and PD-L1 inhibitors (e.g., atezolizumab), work by releasing inhibition of T-cell effector function, thereby resensitizing tumors to the immune response (10). ICIs have shown exceptional clinical benefit across a spectrum of approved indications in solid tumors, but demonstration of broad antitumor activity among hematologic malignancies has been elusive (12).

Similar to solid tumors, diffuse LBCL (DLBCL) may express PD-L1, and tumor PD-L1 expression is associated with inferior survival outcomes (13–16). However, studies of PD-1 inhibitor monotherapy in patients with R/R DLBCL have demonstrated suboptimal and inconsistent outcomes, with ORRs of 3% to 36% (17, 18), and retrospective analysis suggests that some populations of patients with DLBCL [e.g., those with PD-L1 alterations or non–germinal center B-cell (GCB) subtype] may benefit from PD-1/PD-L1 inhibition more than others (19–21). Preclinical data show that anti-CD19 CAR T cells increase the expression of activation markers, including PD-1, after exposure to target antigens (9, 22). Therefore, combining CAR T-cell therapies with an ICI that blocks the PD-1/PD-L1 pathway may serve as a way to improve efficacy by targeting both the antitumor immune response and the tumor itself (10, 23, 24). Here, we report the primary and final analyses of the phase 1/2 ZUMA-6 trial (NCT02926833) investigating the combination of axi-cel with the PD-L1 inhibitor atezolizumab in patients with refractory DLBCL.

sec.title: Study design and patients
sec.p: ZUMA-6 was an open-label, single-arm, multicenter, phase 1/2 study in adult patients with refractory DLBCL conducted at five sites in the United States. A 3 + 3 run-in study design was adopted for phase 1 of ZUMA-6. Patients were monitored for dose-limiting toxicities (DLT) before each additional cohort could proceed with treatment. Patients in phase 2 were enrolled to receive combination treatment with axi-cel and atezolizumab based on the dose and schedule selected from the phase 1 portion of the study as recommended by the safety review team.

Eligible patients were aged ≥18 years with histologically proven DLBCL and refractory disease [defined as primary refractory, no response to ≥2 lines of therapy, or refractory after prior autologous stem cell transplantation (SCT)] who had received adequate therapy, including an anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody and an anthracycline-containing chemotherapy regimen. Key exclusion criteria were prior treatment with a PD-L1 or PD-1 inhibitor or other therapy targeting an immune checkpoint (except for atezolizumab if the patient was eligible for retreatment) or a history of an autoimmune disease (patients with a history of autoimmune-related hypothyroidism on a stable dose of thyroid replacement hormone and patients with controlled type 1 diabetes mellitus on a stable insulin regimen were eligible). Full eligibility criteria are provided in the Supplemental Methods S1.

All patients provided written informed consent, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Good Clinical Practice guideline of the International Conference on Harmonization. The study protocol and amendments were approved by the Institutional Review Board at each site.

sec.title: Treatments and procedures
sec.p: Patients received standard lymphodepleting chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide 500 mg/m2 i.v. and fludarabine 30 mg/m2 i.v.) on days −5 to −3 prior to axi-cel infusion. Axi-cel was administered as a single infusion on day 0 (target dose, 2 × 106 cells/kg). Dosing of lymphodepleting chemotherapy and axi-cel was consistent with the axi-cel label (1). Atezolizumab 1,200 mg i.v. was administered every 21 days for four cycles (to align with the time frame of axi-cel expansion and antitumor activity), with different starting time points evaluated in phase 1 to mitigate potential additive or synergistic toxicities related to the combination regimen. Patients in phase 1 received the first dose of atezolizumab either 21 days (cohort 1), 14 days (cohort 2), or 1 day (cohort 3) after axi-cel infusion. Atezolizumab dosing prior to axi-cel infusion was not considered because of safety precautions. Patients in phase 2 received axi-cel and atezolizumab per the dosing schedule of phase 1 that was determined to have the best overall benefit and safety profile, which was that of cohort 3 (atezolizumab on day 1). Axi-cel was administered to hospitalized patients who were then monitored for ≥7 days after axi-cel infusion. Axi-cel–related toxicities such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS), neurologic events (NE), infections, and cytopenias were managed according to the investigator’s brochure. Atezolizumab-related immune-mediated adverse events (AE) were managed according to standard medical practice.

sec.title: Endpoints and clinical assessments
sec.p: Primary endpoints were the incidence of DLTs (phase 1) and investigator-assessed complete response (CR) rate per the revised International Working Group Response Criteria for Malignant Lymphoma (phase 2; ref. 25). Secondary endpoints included investigator-assessed ORR [CR + partial response (PR)] per the revised International Working Group Response Criteria for Malignant Lymphoma (25), duration of response (DOR), progression-free survival (PFS), OS, safety, and axi-cel and atezolizumab pharmacokinetics (PK) and pharmacodynamics (PD).

Tumor assessments via PET-CT were performed at screening or within 28 days of enrollment, week 6, month 4, month 6, month 9, month 12, and then every 6 months until month 24, followed by every 12 months until month 72. AEs, including NEs, were coded per Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (v21.1) preferred terms and were graded according to the NCI Common Terminology Criteria for AEs (v4.03) and reported until 30 days after the final dose of atezolizumab or 3 months after axi-cel infusion, whichever was longer. CRS events were graded according to a revised grading system by Lee and colleagues (26). DLTs were defined as treatment-related grade 4 hematologic AEs lasting >30 days (except lymphopenia or B-cell aplasia) or all treatment-related grade 3 nonhematologic AEs lasting >7 days and all treatment-related grade 4 nonhematologic AEs regardless of duration (except for prespecified events such as tumor lysis syndrome) with an onset immediately after and through 21 days after the first atezolizumab infusion.

sec.title: Translational assessments
sec.p: Axi-cel concentration in the blood was measured by qPCR, as described previously (27, 28), on day 0 (prior to axi-cel infusion), then weekly through day 28 (phase 2) or day 35 (phase 1 cohort 3), then on days 43, 49, 64, and 69, then in month 3, and then every 3 months to month 18 and month 24; sensitivity of the method was 0.001% or 1 × 10−5. Atezolizumab PK was assessed in blood samples collected (20–40 minutes) after the first atezolizumab infusion was completed, before infusion on atezolizumab treatment days, and ≥90 days following the last infusion. Mass cytometry by time-of-flight (CyTOF) analysis was used to assess CAR T-cell product phenotypes and correlations with clinical outcomes (details included in Supplemental Methods S1) based on 31 markers. Correlative associations of PK, PD, and product characteristics and with clinical outcomes were analyzed using the data cutoff date for the ZUMA-6 final analysis. These analyses were exploratory and/or intended for hypothesis generation. Serum analyte assessment schedule and assays used, measurement of PD-L1 and CD19 expression by IHC, and multiplex immunofluorescence evaluation of tumor immune contexture are described in the Supplemental Methods.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Patients in phase 1 cohort 3 and phase 2 who received axi-cel and ≥1 dose of atezolizumab comprised the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population. The safety analysis set included all patients who received axi-cel. The DLT-evaluable set included all patients in phase 1 who received axi-cel and ≥1 dose of atezolizumab who received the target dose of axi-cel and were followed for ≥21 days after the first atezolizumab infusion. Safety and efficacy endpoints were analyzed descriptively, and the trial was not powered to evaluate a formal statistical hypothesis. The primary analysis was performed after the last patient in the mITT population completed their month 6 assessment. The final analysis was performed after the last treated patient rolled over to the long-term follow-up study. This report includes results of both the primary and final analyses of ZUMA-6.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Between October 2016 and July 2018, 37 patients were enrolled in ZUMA-6 and underwent leukapheresis (Supplementary Fig. S1). Across phase 1 and phase 2, 34 patients received an axi-cel infusion (safety population), and all of these patients subsequently received ≥1 dose of atezolizumab. In cohort 3 of phase 1 and phase 2, 28 patients received axi-cel and ≥1 dose of atezolizumab (mITT population). Among patients who were treated with axi-cel plus atezolizumab, three each were in cohorts 1 and 2 of phase 1, six were in cohort 3 of phase 1, and 22 were in phase 2. Three patients were enrolled but did not receive an axi-cel infusion for reasons that included low platelets (phase 1 cohort 2, n = 1) or AEs (phase 1 cohort 3, n = 1; phase 2, n = 1; Supplementary Results S1). Twenty-four of the 34 patients (71%) completed atezolizumab treatment (four doses); 10 patients had <4 atezolizumab doses for reasons that included AEs (n = 6; Supplementary Results S1), death (due to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome unrelated to study treatment, n = 1), disease progression (n = 2), or an unspecified reason (n = 1). The data cutoff date for the primary analysis was February 21, 2019, with a median follow-up of 10.2 months (range, 6.5–27.9). The data cutoff date for the final analysis was January 12, 2023, with a median follow-up of 56.9 months (range, 53.2–74.6).

The median age among patients who received an axi-cel infusion was 58 years (range, 29–71), 20 patients (59%) were male, and 16 patients (47%) had an Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status of 1 (Table 1; representativeness of study participants is described in Supplementary Table S1). Most patients had stage III/IV disease (n = 26; 76%). Overall, 30 patients (88%) had received ≥2 lines of prior therapy, including 24 (71%) who were refractory to ≥2 lines of therapy and six (18%) who relapsed after prior autologous SCT. The median tumor burden [defined as the sum of product of diameters (SPD)] at baseline was 2,234.23 mm2 (range, 138.32–25,326.00), and the median tumor PD-L1 H-score at baseline was 45 (range, 0–240.0). Most patients (79%) had tumor cells that were PD-L1 positive (PD-L1 H-score >0; n = 27 of 30 evaluable patients).

sec.title: Axi-cel product characteristics
sec.p: Axi-cel product characteristics prior to infusion, including CD4:CD8 ratios and T-cell memory phenotypes, were similar to those of axi-cel in ZUMA-1 (Supplementary Table S2; ref. 29). ZUMA-6 axi-cel products were further characterized using CyTOF panels, including 31 immune cell markers, to characterize the cellular composition of the CAR T-cell products. As expected, non–T-cell markers showed minimal representation: monocytes (CD14; cluster 6), B cells (CD19; cluster 12), and NK cells (CD16 and CD56; cluster 16) each accounted for less than 1.3% of total cells, consistent with the T cell–enriched nature of the product (data not shown). Therefore, we focused our analysis on T-cell populations using markers for lineage (CD3, CD4, and CD8), activation (CD25, HLA-DR, ICOS, OX40, and 4-1BB), late activation/exhaustion (PD-1, TIM-3, LAG-3, and CTLA-4), proliferation (Ki67), and differentiation state (CD27, CD28, CCR7, and CD45RA), cytotoxic potential (NKG2D), and CAR detection (anti-CAR), which are depicted in Supplementary Fig. S2A. The major populations that were observed in axi-cel products were three subsets, each of CD4 and CD8 T cells. CD4+ T cells included one CAR+ subset (cluster 1, 13.02%) with intermediate activation (high CD25, HLA-DR, and ICOS; moderate Ki67; low PD-1, TIM-3, and CD28; and absent CD27) and two CAR− subsets: cluster 2 (7.87%) was more differentiated (high CD28, HLA-DR, CD25, and ICOS; low PD-1 and OX40), whereas cluster 3 (11.91%) was less differentiated (retained CD27 and CD28; expressed CD25 and ICOS; and had negligible HLA-DR, PD-1, and OX40). A minor CAR+ regulatory T-cell cluster (cluster 4, 2.37%) was also present, marked by very high CD25, ICOS, FOXP3, and OX40 (30). Similarly, CD8+ T cells also included one CAR+ subset (cluster 9, 22.54%) with a differentiated cytotoxic profile (high CD25, HLA-DR, and ICOS; moderate NKG2D, TIM-3, and Ki67; and low CD27 and PD-1) and two CAR− subsets: cluster 10 (7.66%) was more differentiated (high CD28, CD25, and ICOS; intermediate HLA-DR, NKG2D, and TIM-3; and low CD27, PD-1, and OX40), whereas cluster 18 (16.31%) was less differentiated (high CD27 and NKG2D; moderate CD25, ICOS, and TIM-3).

sec.title: Primary analysis
sec.p: In phase 1 cohort 3, one patient experienced DLTs (grade 4 neutropenia and grade 4 thrombocytopenia lasting >30 days). All 34 patients in the safety analysis population had treatment-emergent AEs (TEAE) of any grade (Table 2), and 30 (88%) experienced grade ≥3 TEAEs. In phase 2, a grade 5 TEAE occurred on day 43 in one patient because of multiple organ dysfunction secondary to complications from cytomegalovirus pneumonitis and candidemia, which was determined to be unrelated to axi-cel or atezolizumab by the treating physician. The most common grade ≥3 TEAEs were neutropenia/neutrophil count decreased (n = 21; 62%), anemia (n = 20; 59%), and thrombocytopenia/platelet count decreased (n = 13; 38%). The most common grade ≥3 TEAEs are further detailed in Supplementary Table S3. Grade ≥3 TEAEs related to axi-cel, atezolizumab, or both axi-cel and atezolizumab occurred in 50%, 12%, and 21% of patients, respectively. The most common grade ≥3 TEAEs related to both axi-cel and atezolizumab were thrombocytopenia/platelet count decreased (n = 6; 18%), anemia (n = 5; 15%), and neutropenia/neutrophil count decreased (n = 5; 15%). Serious AEs of any grade were reported in 23 patients (68%). Six patients (18%) and two patients (6%) discontinued atezolizumab or had atezolizumab dose delays, respectively, because of grade ≥3 TEAEs.

sec.p: CRS was reported in 33 patients (97%), and grade 3 CRS events occurred in three patients (9%; Table 2); no grade 4 to 5 CRS events were reported. The median time to onset of CRS was 2 days (range, 1–13 days) after axi-cel infusion, and the median duration was 7 days (range, 1–92); all CRS events resolved. Any-grade NEs were reported in 24 patients (71%), and grade ≥3 NEs were reported in 11 patients (32%; Table 2). The median time to onset of NEs was 6 days (range, 1–23 days) after axi-cel infusion, and the median duration was 12 days (range, 2–60). As of the data cutoff date for the primary analysis, NEs resolved in 21 of 24 patients (88%). Two patients had ongoing NEs (grade 1 tremor, n = 1; grade 2 hypoesthesia, n = 1) at the data cutoff date for the primary analysis. One patient with an NE (grade 4 encephalopathy, n = 1) died prior to NE resolution. CRS and NEs were commonly managed with tocilizumab [20 of 33 patients (61%) and nine of 24 patients (38%), respectively] and steroids [eight of 33 patients (24%) and 13 of 24 patients (54%), respectively].

Prolonged cytopenias (present on or after day 30) were reported in 20 patients (59%), including 14 patients (41%) with grade ≥3 events (Table 2). Grade ≥3 prolonged thrombocytopenia and neutropenia occurred in six (18%) and 10 (29%) patients, respectively. Six patients (18%) experienced grade ≥3 prolonged anemia. One patient developed a secondary malignancy of grade 3 melanoma.

Ten patients (29%) died, including eight patients (24%) who died because of disease progression, one patient (3%) who died because of an AE [grade 5 multiple organ dysfunction on day 43 (21 days after their most recent dose of atezolizumab), unrelated to axi-cel or atezolizumab], and one patient (3%) who died because of aseptic meningoencephalitis after withdrawing from the study [related to atezolizumab (95 days after their last dose of atezolizumab)].

sec.title: Final analysis
sec.p: After the primary analysis data cutoff date, six patients (18%) experienced new TEAEs that occurred >6 months after axi-cel infusion. Grade 3 serious TEAEs occurred in two patients (urinary tract infection, n = 1; acute kidney injury and influenza A infection, n = 1). No new TEAEs related to axi-cel were reported. Grade 1 to 2 TEAEs deemed by the investigator to be related to atezolizumab were reported in two patients (lichen nitidus, n = 1; hypothyroidism and cognitive disorder, n = 1). Grade 1 to 2 TEAEs that were not related to treatment were reported in two patients.

Eight additional patients died, including three patients who died because of disease progression and four patients who died because of other reasons [sepsis, neutropenic sepsis, COVID-19–related complications, secondary myelodysplastic syndrome (with a clinically significant TP53 variant detected at leukapheresis); n = 1 each]. Lymphocyte and neutrophil counts over time in the three patients who died because of infections are depicted in Supplementary Fig. S3. One patient who had an unresolved NE of grade 2 hypoesthesia (ongoing prior to the data cutoff date for the primary analysis) died of unknown causes.

sec.title: Primary analysis
sec.p: At the data cutoff date for the primary analysis, 21 of 28 patients [75%; 95% confidence interval (CI), 55%–89%] in the mITT population achieved an investigator-assessed objective response, and 13 patients (46%) had a best overall response of CR with axi-cel in combination with atezolizumab (Supplementary Table S4). One patient had a late conversion to CR (from PR at day 107; Supplementary Fig. S4). The proportion of patients with a response who remained in response at month 12 was 61.9% (95% CI, 38.1%–78.8%), and the 12-month PFS rate was 50% (95% CI, 30.6%–66.6%). The median DOR and PFS were not reached as of the data cutoff date for the primary analysis. At 12 months, the OS rate was 71.4% (95% CI, 50.9%–84.6%); the median OS was not reached. Overall, seven of the 34 patients (21%) who were treated with axi-cel plus atezolizumab across all cohorts received subsequent anti-lymphoma therapies after disease progression.

sec.title: Final analysis
sec.p: As of the final analysis data cutoff date, 15 patients (54%) in the mITT population had a best overall response of CR (Fig. 1A); investigator-assessed ORR was unchanged from the primary analysis. Individual responses and survival status over time are presented in Fig. 1B. Late CR conversions occurred in two additional patients (PR to CR at days 272 and 1,080; Supplementary Fig. S4). Three additional patients in cohorts 1 and 2 of phase 1 (who were not in the mITT population) achieved late CR conversions (PR/stable disease to CR at days 176, 265, and 281).

sec.p: The median DOR was 41.4 months (95% CI, 1.8–not estimable; Fig. 2A). Among patients with a response (n = 21), nine patients (43%) had ongoing responses at the final analysis data cutoff date. The median PFS was 9 months (95% CI, 3.1–not estimable; Fig. 2B), and the 48-month PFS rate was 31.5% (95% CI, 14.2%–50.4%). The median OS was 32.2 months (95% CI, 11.6–not estimable; Fig. 2C), and the 48-month OS rate was 40.7% (95% CI, 22.1%–58.6%). Four additional patients of 34 (12%) received subsequent anti-lymphoma therapies (in between the data cutoff dates for the primary and final analyses), including one patient who had an allogeneic SCT (195 days after their last dose of atezolizumab).

sec.title: PK and PD
sec.p: The median peak CAR T-cell levels [37.29 cells/μL (range, 0.08–195.50)] and the median time to peak CAR T-cell expansion [8 days (range, 8–273)] in the mITT population (phase 1 cohort 3 and phase 2) were comparable with those observed with axi-cel monotherapy in ZUMA-1 cohort 1 (patients with LBCL; Fig. 3A). Atezolizumab infusions did not appear to significantly affect the median peak CAR T-cell expansion or persistence over time when compared with axi-cel monotherapy in ZUMA-1 cohort 1 (Fig. 3A). Patients in cohorts 1 and 2 (n = 3 each; not included in the mITT population) who received offset atezolizumab dosing (on day 21 and day 14, respectively) after peak CAR T-cell expansion may have had higher peak expansion compared with the mITT population, but differences were not significant with low sample size in these two cohorts (Supplementary Fig. S5A and S5B) and a wide range of baseline disease burden across all cohorts (Supplementary Fig. S5C). The median CAR T-cell AUC values from days 0 to 28/35 [AUC0–28/35; 496.68 cells/μL*days (range, 1.93 × 10−3–2,221.56)] and AUC0–90 [628.01 cells/μL*days (range, 0.75–2,658.81)] in the ZUMA-6 mITT population were also consistent with those reported for ZUMA-1 cohort 1 (Fig. 3B). Among the six patients who had late conversions to CR across all ZUMA-6 cohorts (days 107–1,080), four had detectable CAR T-cell levels at the time of late CR (Supplementary Fig. S4).

sec.p: CAR T-cell expansion (peak or AUC) in patients in the mITT population who had an objective response (n = 21) was not significantly different from patients who did not have a response (n = 7; Supplementary Fig. S6A). There was also no apparent relationship between median peak CAR T-cell expansion and baseline tumor burden (as measured as sum of the product of diameters). However, higher median CAR T-cell AUC values were observed in patients with grade ≥3 NEs versus those with grade ≤2 NEs (P = 0.0157; Supplementary Fig. S6B); a similar trend was also observed in patients with grade ≥2 NEs versus those with grade ≤1 NEs (P = 0.0581). CAR T-cell expansion did not appear to associate with CRS severity (Supplementary Fig. S6C).

Patients with a response also tended to have a higher cumulative dose of atezolizumab (i.e., consistent with remaining on study and continued atezolizumab dosing; Supplementary Fig. S7A). When adjusted for total cumulative dose of atezolizumab using logistic regression, there was no association between objective response and concentrations of atezolizumab (AUC0–64) in the blood (P = 0.2053); unadjusted comparisons are shown in Supplementary Fig. S7B).

sec.title: Preinfusion axi-cel CAR T-cell phenotypes and clinical outcomes
sec.p: T-cell phenotypes in axi-cel products prior to infusion were analyzed by CyTOF for associations with objective responses and grade ≥3 NEs (although with low numbers of nonresponders and patients with grade ≥3 NEs; Supplementary Fig. S2B). There were no significant differences in the major six T-cell clusters identified in axi-cel products described above with respect to responses or grade ≥3 NEs. Overall, patients who did not have a response (n = 7) had higher frequencies of more differentiated cytotoxic CD8 T cells compared with those who had a response, including both CAR+ (cluster 9) and CAR− (cluster 10) populations. Notably, elevated levels of differentiated CAR+ T cells (cluster 9) were also observed in patients who experienced grade ≥3 NEs (n = 8) compared with those who had grade ≤2 NEs. These analyses were limited by small sample size and the overlap between groups—specifically, three of the eight patients with grade ≥3 NEs were also patients without a response.

sec.title: Biomarker analysis
sec.p: PD-L1 and CD19 target expression was measured by histology (H-score for PD-L1 and CD19; %PD-L1+ for PD-L1) on pretreatment tumor biopsies from 25 patients in the mITT population (Supplementary Fig. S8A and S8B). Although most patients (79%) were positive for tumor PD-L1 expression (H-score >0) prior to infusion, the median expression levels on a per biopsy basis were low (median H-score, 45.0). There was no association between either PD-L1 (by H-score or %PD-L1+ tumor cells) or CD19 with objective responses in these patients. The median overall baseline tumor burden (sum of the product of diameters) was numerically lower in patients with response compared with those without response (Supplementary Fig. S8C). There was a correlation between pretreatment PD-L1 expression and baseline serum concentrations of soluble PD-L1 (Spearman correlation, 0.5837; P < 0.001; Supplementary Fig. S9). Serum concentrations of most key analytes, including proinflammatory and immunomodulatory cytokines, were consistent with previous studies of axi-cel monotherapy (Supplemental Results S1; Supplementary Table S5; Supplementary Fig. S10; associations with CRS/NEs described in Supplementary Table S6).

sec.title: Tumor immune contexture
sec.p: Baseline tumor samples from up to 15 patients in the mITT population were further analyzed using a multiplexed immunofluorescence staining assay to describe the pretreatment endogenous immune contexture. PAX5+ B cells were the most prevalent cell population, with a median frequency of 72% (IQR, 48%–79%; Supplementary Fig. S11). The median frequencies of T cells (CD4+ or CD8+) and nonlymphocytes (PAX5− CD4− CD8−) were 18% (IQR, 12%–25%) and 12% (IQR, 6%–28%), respectively. Generally, the frequency of PD-L1–positive cells present in the tumor microenvironment was low (median, 0.11%; IQR, 0.02%–17%), and most of these cells also had myeloid lineage markers (e.g., CD11c). The nonlymphocyte population primarily comprised cells of the macrophage/monocyte lineage or dendritic cells (CD68+, CD163+, or CD11c+), with a smaller proportion of CD31+ endothelial cells detected. Separately, the expression of T-cell immunomodulatory and regulatory markers was measured in baseline tumor samples from 15 patients in the mITT population. The median frequency of PD-1+ cells was 12% (IQR, 3%–17%) and the median frequencies of FOXP3+ and LAG-3+ cells were 1% (IQR, 1%–2%) and 2% (IQR, 1%–4%), respectively.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Axi-cel has significantly improved survival outcomes in patients with R/R LBCL (5, 6); however, long-term outcomes highlight the need for further improvement. It is hypothesized that PD-1/PD-L1 signaling in CAR T cells may adversely affect long-term responses in this patient population (22, 24). ZUMA-6 evaluated the safety and efficacy of axi-cel in combination with the PD-L1 inhibitor atezolizumab in patients with refractory DLBCL. Despite concurrent blockade of the inhibitory PD-1/PD-L1 pathway in axi-cel and endogenous T cells, the efficacy of axi-cel plus atezolizumab was comparable with that observed for axi-cel monotherapy in the ZUMA-1 trial (5, 29). Although proinflammatory pathways that contribute to atezolizumab-related immune-mediated AEs had the potential to overlap with CAR T cell–related toxicities (e.g., CRS and NEs; refs. 31, 32), the safety profile reported in ZUMA-6 was generally consistent with that of ZUMA-1, and no new safety signals were observed (29).

Owing to the function of atezolizumab as a PD-L1 inhibitor targeting T-cell exhaustion, we hypothesized that the addition of atezolizumab to axi-cel therapy would improve CAR T-cell expansion and persistence, as well as the antitumor activity of both CAR T cells and endogenous T cells. However, peak CAR T-cell expansion and persistence in patients treated with axi-cel plus atezolizumab were comparable with those who received axi-cel monotherapy in ZUMA-1. The elevated cytokine profiles that were anticipated in patients treated with combination therapy in ZUMA-6 were instead similar to those observed with monotherapy in ZUMA-1 (29, 33), including comparable levels of cytotoxic T-cell effector molecules (i.e., granzyme B and IFNγ; ref. 34). Interestingly, there was no association between CAR T-cell expansion and durable remission in ZUMA-6 unlike reports on axi-cel monotherapy (28). The addition of atezolizumab may possibly neutralize the negative prognostic impact of suboptimal expansion; however, the small number of nonresponders precludes a definitive interpretation.

ZUMA-6 and ZUMA-1 were separate, single-arm studies with differences in study design (i.e., primary endpoints and trial size); therefore, comparisons of efficacy outcomes between axi-cel plus atezolizumab and axi-cel monotherapy are qualitative and should be interpreted as exploratory. In addition to DLBCL, ZUMA-1 also enrolled patients with primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma or transformed follicular lymphoma; however, baseline characteristics of ZUMA-6 were generally comparable with the DLBCL cohort of ZUMA-1 (29). With a median follow-up time of 56.9 months, nine of 21 patients (43%) who had an objective response with axi-cel plus atezolizumab had an ongoing response, suggesting that combination therapy did not have a significant impact on enhancement of durable responses compared with axi-cel monotherapy in ZUMA-1 (ongoing responses in 31% of patients with a response; median follow-up, 63.1 months; refs. 5, 29). The CR rate among patients in ZUMA-6 (54%) was also similar when compared with ZUMA-1 (49% in patients with DLBCL; ref. 29). Overall, late CR conversions did not occur more frequently in ZUMA-6 than what was observed in ZUMA-1 (29, 35); six patients had late CR conversions, and three of those patients had detectable CAR T-cell levels beyond month 12. However, it is possible that late conversions may reflect limitations of PET-/CT-based imaging that can misconstrue resolution of necrotic lesions with that of potential residual disease (36). The lack of increased efficacy observed with axi-cel plus atezolizumab compared with axi-cel monotherapy in ZUMA-1 is consistent with the generally favorable safety profile observed in ZUMA-6 (29).

The safety and cytokine profiles in this study were consistent with the lack of an additive or synergistic effect of atezolizumab on either axi-cel efficacy or endogenous T-cell activity. By CyTOF analysis, axi-cel product cells expressed low levels of PD-1 prior to infusion. Although sustained expression of PD-1 on the surface of endogenous T cells generally occurs with persistent exposure to antigens (37, 38), expression on CAR T cells can be quickly induced following exposure to antigens (9, 22), the kinetics of which may be critical for the treatment effect of atezolizumab (39). Atezolizumab dosing prior to axi-cel infusion was not tested because of safety considerations, and some patients (cohorts 1 and 2 of phase 1) did not receive atezolizumab until day 21 or 14 per study design. Furthermore, owing to their design, CAR T cells do not require antigen-presenting cells to receive costimulatory signals (40), and therefore, interactions with PD-L1–expressing cells may not be a limiting step for expansion and antitumor activity, potentially reducing the significance of this pathway in CAR T cells.

Due to the heterogeneous nature of T-cell exhaustion and the role that both the tumor microenvironment and the patient’s peripheral immune system play in T-cell exhaustion, the small, unselected (i.e., with regard to DLBCL subtype) patient population in this study may not have been sufficient to observe an atezolizumab-mediated benefit on T-cell exhaustion (37, 41–43). Patients included in ZUMA-6 may not have been those with the greatest potential to benefit from inhibition of the PD-1/PD-L1 signaling axis due to tumor genomics or PD-L1 expression patterns. Although 79% of patients had detectable baseline tumor PD-L1, the median H-score was 45 of a possible 300. PD-L1 alterations in DLBCL tumors have been associated with a clinical response to PD-1 blockade, and increased tumor PD-L1 expression in DLBCL has been associated with the non-GCB subtype (19–21). However, patients were not screened for PD-L1 alterations and only a small proportion in ZUMA-6 had non-GCB DLBCL. It is possible that the combination of atezolizumab and axi-cel could have a greater impact in populations of patients with non-GCB DLBCL, but this would require a separately designed study. Another potential limitation of the study design of ZUMA-6 was that the protocol-defined assessment schedule may not have included the ideal time points with which to observe a transient atezolizumab-mediated effect on CAR T-cell or cytokine levels, thereby limiting some mechanistic insights. Finally, interactions between PD-1 and PD-L2 may have contributed to T-cell exhaustion, bypassing the atezolizumab-mediated inhibition of the PD-1/PD-L1 signaling pathway (44). As a PD-L1 inhibitor, atezolizumab was selected, in part, because of a lower risk of toxicities/NEs compared with PD-1 inhibitors. However, inhibition of PD-1 instead of PD-L1 may offer better outcomes in patients with DLBCL who receive CAR T-cell therapies.

Although synergistic effects were not observed with axi-cel plus atezolizumab, immune checkpoint blockade remains a potential avenue for further study in subsets of patients with hematologic malignancies. Findings from ZUMA-6 suggest that the safety profile of atezolizumab in combination with axi-cel was manageable; therefore, investigation of this combination could be considered in patients who may benefit from PD-1 blockade (i.e., those with primary mediastinal B-cell lymphoma tumors that express PD-L1; ref. 45). Studies are ongoing in patients with lymphomas to evaluate the impact of anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy in combination with other ICIs, including durvalumab, pembrolizumab, and newer agents such as relatlimab, which target pathways that could be more relevant for CAR T-cell activity (e.g., LAG-3; refs. 46, 47). Although early-phase studies have thus far not found an extended clinical benefit compared with CAR T-cell monotherapy (39, 48), findings from ZUMA-6 may help inform the study design of future trials of CAR T-cell combinations with ICIs.

sec.title: Data Availability Statement
sec.p: Gilead Sciences shares anonymized individual participant data upon request or as required by law or regulation with qualified external researchers based on submitted curriculum vitae and reflecting non–conflict of interest. The request proposal must also include a statistician. Approval of such requests is at Gilead Science’s discretion and is dependent on the nature of the request, the merit of the research proposed, the availability of the data, and the intended use of the data. Data requests should be sent to datasharing@gilead.com.
